chapters.title: Book Three: THE SEA CAPTAIN'S PORTRAIT

spans.text: For the whispers the sea keeps, and the ones it finally gives back.
CHAPTER ONE: THE GINGER MAE
Adley Brindendale was found face-down in his driveway on a wet Tuesday morning in June. He was wearing his good boots. The coroner said he had fallen.
The coroner was wrong.

The ferry from Cedar Point made the crossing in forty minutes on a calm day, and this was a calm day, the kind Patchogu Island arranged for itself in late May before the summer tourists arrived to complicate everything. The water was flat and pearl-grey, the horizon a soft smudge where the Atlantic absorbed the sky, and the island materialized the way it always did for Victoria Laine: not as a destination, but as a correction. Like the world had been slightly wrong since she left, and now, rounding into the channel, it was adjusting itself back.

She stood at the bow railing while Olivia sat cross-legged on a bench behind her eating a gas station bag of peanut butter crackers and Solei read something on her phone with the focused silence of a person who was actually thinking rather than scrolling. The three of them had driven down from Raleigh that morning, crammed into Olivia's Jeep, and barely spoken for the last hour of it, the comfortable kind of quiet that only existed between people who had known each other long enough that silence wasn't awkward, it was just weather.
You're doing the thing,
spans.speaker: Olivia

spans.text: Olivia said.
Victoria didn't turn around.
What thing.
spans.speaker: Victoria

spans.text: The standing-at-the-bow thing. Like you're on the Titanic.
I'm looking at the island.
You're being cinematic.
spans.speaker: Olivia

spans.text: Olivia crunched a cracker.
There's a difference.
spans.speaker: Olivia

spans.text: Solei looked up from her phone.
She's been doing it since the Outer Banks bridge. I clocked it.
spans.speaker: Solei

spans.text: Victoria turned around, and because they were both watching her with the particular expression they reserved for moments they planned to remember and weaponize later, she smiled. It was a good smile; she knew that, had known it since ninth grade, which was both a gift and a problem she was still working out.
I'm glad to be back,
spans.speaker: Victoria

spans.text: she said.
Is that allowed?
spans.speaker: Victoria

spans.text: Completely allowed,
spans.speaker: Olivia

spans.text: Olivia said.
Just do it with less hair.
spans.speaker: Olivia

spans.text: The wind off the water was cold enough to keep the gulls honest, and they hung above the ferry in loose, wheeling clusters, crying out with the specific urgency of birds who had important opinions about nothing. Patchogu Island was six miles long and barely two miles wide at its broadest point, a low, sandy crescent of a place that had decided sometime around 1890 to stop caring what the mainland thought of it. There were dunes and sea oats and weathered cedar houses set back from the water. There was a lighthouse at the north end that had guided ships since before the Civil War and now mostly guided tourists with cameras. There was one school, one post office, two churches that hadn't spoken to each other in forty years over a dispute no one under sixty could fully remember, a hardware store that also sold bait, and, at the corner of Tidal Bay Road and North Main Street, the Ginger Mae Coffee Shop.
This was where they were going. This was, to varying degrees and in varying ways, what they were going back for.
Grandma Knapp was not, technically, anyone's grandmother.

The title was honorific, given years ago by the island's collective instinct for the right word. Her actual name was Ginger Mae Knapp (the shop was named after her, not the other way around) and she had run it alone since her husband Harold passed in 2001, and somewhat less alone since Victoria, Olivia, and Solei had started spending their summers on the island as teenagers and gradually, naturally, indispensably taken up positions in the daily operations. By now, in their late twenties,
"helping Grandma at the shop"
had become
"running the shop while Grandma supervised from her stool behind the counter and told them they were doing it wrong."
The arrangement suited everyone.

Victoria had a key to the shop's back door. She also had a key to Grandma's cottage on the dune, and to the storage shed, and to the lockbox where the quarterly tax documents lived, and to the small fireproof safe inside the supply closet where Grandma kept the recipe notebooks. The safe key was the only one that ever made Grandma pause before handing it over. For emergencies, she'd said, pressing it into Victoria's palm three summers ago, her grip dry and precise as paper. Don't go rummaging in there out of boredom.

Victoria had not gone rummaging. But she thought about it sometimes. She had thought she knew Grandma Knapp. She had been thinking this for twelve years. It was possible this was the wrong thought to have been having.

The Ginger Mae was not a large place: eight tables inside, four on the porch when the weather allowed, a counter with six stools, and a kitchen that produced exactly what it intended to: scones, muffins, three kinds of soup in rotation, and coffee so consistent and quietly exceptional that people drove from the mainland on weekends just to sit with a cup of it and read the newspaper the old way, on actual paper, which Grandma stocked in a rack by the door and which she charged for on the honor system.

The tea was self-service. You sidled up to a wooden rack of small labeled tins, chamomile, peppermint, hibiscus, bergamot, ginger, each in a squat round tin with a paper label in Grandma Knapp's handwriting, the ink faded from handling, the lids polished bright from the same, and you selected what you wanted and brought it back to your table and Grandma or whoever was working would bring hot water. It was a small thing, but it was the kind of small thing that gave a place character. People liked choosing their own tea. It felt like being trusted.
What the Ginger Mae was not, this May, was doing well.

Olivia had the numbers. She always had the numbers; she was the one who'd gone to business school and come back smelling of spreadsheets and a briefly held conviction that they could triple revenue with a mobile ordering app. Victoria had talked her down off that ledge, but the numbers remained, and Olivia had sent them to the other two in a shared document two weeks before the drive down, with a note that said only: Read before you get here. We need to talk.

Victoria had read them on her couch in Raleigh with a glass of wine she kept refilling without fully registering it. The short version: the Ginger Mae was losing money. Not catastrophically, not dramatically, but steadily and in the particular way that was actually worse, the slow kind, where you could tell yourself each month that next month would be different.
The longer version involved the Septuagenarian Club.

For more than twenty years, a group of the island's elder residents had convened at the Ginger Mae at precisely eight-thirty in the morning, six days a week. They called themselves the Septuagenarian Club, though several of them had long since aged past that designation and no one had updated the name. At their peak there had been ten of them; now there were six, which was the arithmetic of old age, unavoidable and unkind. They occupied the four-top by the window and, on Saturdays, pushed it together with the adjacent table to accommodate whatever family members were visiting. They had strong opinions about the county fair judging, several of them owned galleries that sold well to tourists, and their collective presence in the Ginger Mae every morning had functioned for decades as a kind of endorsement, the social equivalent of a Michelin star, island-specific and entirely unspoken.
They had, without warning or explanation, stopped coming.

This had happened eighteen months ago. One Tuesday they were there; the following Tuesday they were not. By Wednesday of that week they had apparently transferred their allegiance to Pandora's Box, a newer coffee shop three blocks over run by a woman named Tara Finch who had moved to the island from Charlotte seven years ago and who, according to island consensus, made a mediocre cortado and an excellent show of listening to whoever was talking. The Septuagenarian Club had been going to Pandora's Box every morning since.
Nobody had explained it. Grandma Knapp had not asked.
This was, to Victoria's mind, the strangest part.

The ferry docked with the particular thud that meant home, and they hauled their bags down the gangway and into the brightness of the late-May morning. The island smelled like salt and cut grass and something else underneath, old wood warming in the sun, or the cedar shingles releasing the winter's cold, or simply the smell of Patchogu Island that had no name and needed none.

Olivia's Jeep was waiting in the lot where she'd pre-arranged to have it trailered over the week before. They loaded their bags and drove the four blocks to the Ginger Mae, four blocks being the distance you drove on Patchogu Island when you had luggage and a reason, and because Victoria wanted to see it before she saw the cottage.

It looked the same. It always looked the same: the cedar shingles gone silver-grey, the hand-lettered sign above the door with its little painted ginger blossom, the chalkboard on the sidewalk where the daily soup was written in Grandma's handwriting that had not meaningfully changed in forty years. Tuesday: Clam chowder. Bread today: rosemary. The porch furniture had been brought out for the season, the cushions a faded nautical stripe that had been fading for so long they had arrived at a kind of permanent, intentional-looking paleness. A basket of sea lavender hung by the door.
Same,
spans.speaker: Olivia

spans.text: Olivia said, pulling up.
Same,
spans.speaker: Victoria

spans.text: Victoria agreed, which was not a criticism.
Solei got out without a word and stood looking at the shop with an expression that might have been affection or might have been calculation, and was probably both. Then she said,
"The gutter on the left is loose,"
and went inside.

Grandma Knapp was at her stool behind the counter, which was where she always was when they arrived, as if she had not moved since they'd left the previous September but had simply sat in patient suspension, waiting. She was eighty-one, small and wire-thin, her white hair pinned up in its usual knot, wearing an apron that said Ginger Mae across the front (the name of the shop, and for all practical purposes her own name, since no one on Patchogu Island had called her Marjorie in forty years; Corey had been her name before Knapp, and before that it had belonged to her father, and before that to the sea captain grandfather she'd never met but whose portrait hung in the back hallway) and a cardigan the color of old mustard that Victoria was fairly certain had been a fixture of this kitchen since the Clinton administration.

She looked up when they came through the door and her face did the thing it did: the small, involuntary brightening, quickly composed, as if being too visibly glad was a form of vulnerability she preferred not to display.
Well,
she said.
You're here.
We're here,
spans.speaker: Victoria

spans.text: Victoria said, and went around the counter and hugged her, which Grandma tolerated with the brief, sincere squeeze that was her version of an embrace. She smelled like cinnamon and coffee and the faintest trace of lavender water.
Olivia came in behind her, already scanning the kitchen with a proprietorial eye.
Did you restock the chamomile? I sent you the order.
spans.speaker: Olivia

spans.text: The chamomile is fine,
spans.speaker: Grandma

spans.text: Grandma said.
It was down to two tins.
Two tins is sufficient for a Tuesday in May.
spans.speaker: Grandma

spans.text: Grandma Knapp picked up her coffee mug and held it in both hands the way she did when she wanted to end a line of conversation.

The clam chowder is on the stove. The bread needs another twenty minutes. Adley will be here at eight-thirty and he'll want his scone warmed, not toasted, which is a distinction I suspect has been lost on whoever has been filling in since March.
spans.speaker: Grandma

spans.text: We've been briefing Carla,
spans.speaker: Victoria

spans.text: Victoria said.
Carla,
spans.speaker: Grandma

spans.text: Grandma repeated, in the tone she used for things she found unnecessary.
She's been very good.
She warms the scones too long. Adley hasn't complained because Adley doesn't complain about things, but I can tell.

Victoria exchanged a glance with Olivia over Grandma's head. This was the thing about Grandma Knapp: she noticed everything about her regulars with a precision that would have been remarkable in anyone, and was frankly bewildering in an eighty-one-year-old woman who had, for the past two winters, shown signs of a memory that was beginning to do what memories do at a certain age, which was drift.

The drifting had started small: a word misplaced, a name temporarily unavailable, the occasional sentence that lost its thread halfway through and then recovered it somewhere unexpected. Victoria's mother had said not to make too much of it, that everyone's grandmother did this, that it was normal. Victoria's mother had also, in the same conversation, admitted she hadn't visited Patchogu in two years, so her reassurances carried limited weight.

What concerned Victoria more than the forgetting was the remembering: the vivid, disorganized way Grandma Knapp had begun talking about a past that seemed to bear only an approximate relationship to her actual life. She spoke of Paris, which so far as any of them knew she had never visited. She spoke of a speakeasy her father had taken her to, which was possible but felt embellished. She described, in cinematic detail, a man being chased through an alley by two other men while she watched from a fire escape, which was not the sort of thing that happened to a woman from a barrier island off the coast of North Carolina unless her life had been considerably more eventful than advertised.
Solei had a theory about this. She had arrived at it, as she arrived at most things, obliquely and without announcing herself. But that conversation was for later.

In the meantime, she had restocked the chamomile (three tins, because Olivia's order had been correct and Grandma's confidence in two tins had not) and was standing at the tea rack in the way she stood at most things she found worth examining: with a stillness that was not passivity but attention, the way a person listens when they have decided the thing they're listening to has something to say. The rack was old cedar, the joints dark with decades of steam and handling. She had noticed on her first morning back that the bottom-right corner had begun to separate, not urgently, not yet, but the wood was communicating its intentions if you were inclined to notice. She would need to fix it before the separation became a split, and a split became a loose tin, and a loose tin became a customer with a lapful of bergamot.
She added it to the list she kept in her notebook. The list was mostly small things. She had learned, early, that small things were the ones worth keeping track of.

By eight-fifteen the shop had three tables occupied: a young couple from the mainland who had driven over for the weekend and who consulted their phones throughout their meal with the commitment of people who required documentation of all experiences; an older woman named Harriet Bale who had lived on the island her whole life and came in every Tuesday for the chowder; and a man at the window table reading a folded copy of the Patchogu Prattler who Victoria didn't immediately recognize, then did: Dale Symons, retired harbormaster, who'd been coming in on and off for years and whom she had known since she was seventeen without ever having had a conversation with him that lasted more than four minutes.

The Septuagenarian Club's table sat empty. It would stay empty. The four-top by the window had developed, in their absence, the mute, slightly accusatory quality of a table that knows it has been stood up and has not gotten over it.
Olivia stood behind the counter slicing rosemary bread and not looking at the table. Victoria noticed that she was not looking at it.
At eight twenty-seven, the bell above the door sounded and Adley Brindendale came in.

He was seventy-eight and built like a man who had once been considerably larger and had weathered down to something essential, the way coastline weathers, less material, but more defined. He had white hair he didn't bother much about, a face that had been sun-damaged for so long it had settled into a kind of permanent weathered dignity, and he walked with a slight list to the left that he'd had since a horse had taken exception to him about a decade ago. He wore his usual: dark trousers, a linen shirt the color of oatmeal, and boots that had probably been expensive once and were now simply good.
Ladies,
he said.
Mr. Brindendale,
spans.speaker: Victoria

spans.text: Victoria said, which was what she always said, though he'd told her a hundred times to call him Adley.
You're back.

He settled onto his stool at the counter (the third one from the left, always) and folded his hands on the wood in front of him. He had large, well-kept hands, the hands of a man who had used them for things other than paperwork, though paperwork had apparently also featured. The story of Adley Brindendale, assembled over years from the island's collective account of itself, was this: he had been born on Patchogu, left young, made money somewhere in Florida as a lawyer and then as something else not entirely specified, and returned to the island in his late sixties to spend his remaining years in peace. He had bought a six-bedroom house on the north end, more house than a man alone needed, and filled its barn with the classic cars he'd apparently spent decades acquiring and now maintained with devoted, meticulous care. He was known to be generous to local nonprofits, occasionally cantankerous to contractors, unfailingly polite to women, and dismissive of any suggestion that his health was anything other than excellent.
